content: The term index case or primary case refers to the first identified patient in an epidemiological investigation. This patient is the initial case of a disease or condition within a population, or the first case described in medical literature, even if they are not necessarily the first person affected. The index case can provide critical information about the source of the disease, its potential spread, and the reservoir where the disease persists between outbreaks. In some instances, the index case becomes a classic case in medical literature, such as the case of Phineas Gage. The index case is often the first indication of an outbreak, although earlier cases may later be identified and classified as primary, secondary, tertiary, and so on. The term Patient Zero has been used to describe the index case in the context of the HIV epidemic in North America. In genetics, the index case, also known as the propositus or proband, is the first patient whose condition prompts the investigation of other family members for potential genetic factors. The Case of Gaëtan Dugas (Patient Zero) During the early years of the AIDS epidemic, an epidemiological study led by Dr. William Darrow and colleagues at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) identified a Patient Zero scenario. This study demonstrated how one individual had transmitted HIV to multiple sexual partners, who then spread the virus further, leading to its rapid dissemination across the globe (Auerbach et al., 1984). The CDC identified Gaëtan Dugas, a flight attendant, as a carrier of the virus from Africa to the United States. He was reported to have spread HIV to other men he encountered in gay bathhouses. Journalist Randy Shilts popularized the term Patient Zero in his 1987 book And the Band Played On, which portrayed Dugas as a central figure in the early spread of HIV among homosexual men in North America. Shilts described Dugas as being sexually promiscuous in various North American cities. For years, Dugas was vilified as a mass spreader of HIV and was wrongly perceived as the original source of the epidemic. However, four years later, Dr. Darrow criticized the study's methodology and the way Shilts had represented its findings. In 2007, a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by Michael Worobey and Dr. Arthur Pitchenik used genetic analysis to suggest that HIV likely entered the United States from Africa via Haiti around 1969, likely through a single immigrant. Furthermore, Robert Rayford, a teenager who died in St. Louis, Missouri, in 1969 from complications of AIDS, was likely infected as early as 1966, indicating that there were earlier carriers of HIV in North America. The term Patient Zero has since been adopted more broadly in the media to describe the index case in infectious disease outbreaks, computer virus outbreaks, and even as a metaphor for the origin of ideas or actions with widespread consequences. Other Notable Index Cases Mary Mallon (Typhoid Mary): Mary Mallon was an asymptomatic carrier of typhoid fever who infected 47 people while working as a cook. She was eventually quarantined to prevent further spread of the disease. Mabalo Lokela (Ebola Virus): The first recorded victim of the Ebola virus was a 44-year-old schoolteacher named Mabalo Lokela, who died on September 8, 1976, 14 days after the onset of symptoms. Liu Jianlun (SARS): A 64-year-old doctor from Guangdong, Liu Jianlun, transmitted SARS during his stay at the Metropole Hotel in Hong Kong in 2003, contributing to the global spread of the disease. 1854 Cholera Outbreak in London: A baby living in the Lewis House at 40 Broad Street is considered the index patient in the cholera outbreak in Soho, London, as described in Steven Johnson's book The Ghost Map. Édgar Enrique Hernández (2009 Swine Flu): Édgar Enrique Hernández, a young boy, is believed to be the index case of the 2009 swine flu outbreak. He survived the illness, and a bronze statue was erected in his honor. Maria Adela Gutierrez, who contracted the virus around the same time, became the first officially confirmed fatality of the outbreak. Related Terms Proband: The first affected individual in a family who brings a genetic disorder to medical attention. Mayinga N'Seka: A nurse who became an index case during an Ebola outbreak.
